blindSummary: This is one of the most tolerant jurisdictions in its region for transgender visitors, on par with the region's most protective legal tier. Same-sex relations are legal; employment discrimination based on sexual orientation is prohibited; the capital and the second city host visible Pride events; the culture is notably relaxed by regional standards. There are no explicit gender-identity protections and no legal-gender-recognition statute (administrative practice unclear), but there is no documented anti-trans violence pattern.
blindOutOfScope: The legal-gender-recognition statute gap is noted; the evidence base is thin but consistent.
blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations not criminalised in this country; employment protections based on sexual orientation (though gender identity/expression/sex characteristics not explicitly referenced); first Pride in 2013 - the second country in its region to host one; 82% public acceptance of a 'homosexual' neighbour (2019-2021 polls); LGBTIQ organisations can register; no same-sex union recognition; committed at its 2024 UPR to improve protections; one of only two countries from its region in the UN member-state core group on LGBTI rights.

Equality-monitoring project (July 2018): this country's LGBTI Pride week in the capital - supported by the government's gender-equality institute, a foreign development agency and the city administration; Pride began in the second city in 2013; activists campaign for same-sex marriage and an anti-LGBTIphobia non-discrimination law; the march's slogan is roughly 'at ease with who I am'.
NOTE: this is a foreign government's archived human-rights reports index page (navigation only); the specific report on this country was not retrievable.

Foreign daily and news agency (July 2017): this country's prime minister said same-sex marriage is not on the government's political agenda, calling it 'opinion' - responding to LGBT community claims to union and marriage rights.

Continental attitudes-survey dispatch no. 362 (May 2020) - a survey on tolerance of differences finds respondents across the continent are tolerant on ethnic, religious and national differences but not sexual differences; this country, together with two regional peers, stands out as particularly tolerant; tolerance toward sexual minorities remains remarkably weak even among younger respondents.

Regional magazine special (June 2016): interview with the first person to come out publicly as trans in this country (1997, during the second city's carnival) - describes the country as relatively free for its small LGBT community, the second city as relaxed, though she personally experienced verbal violence and two physical attacks (possibly robbery-motivated).
blindLocalsOnly: No explicit gender-identity protections and no legal-gender-recognition statute (administrative practice unclear) — resident-facing gaps.
blindTangential: Same-sex relations legal and employment discrimination prohibited — no partner-related exposure for visitors.
